title: Solve common SDET coding tasks and state complexity/edge cases — first non-repeating character, reverse a string without built-ins, remove duplicates from an array (and the follow-up: dedupe objects by a specific property), and second-highest salary in SQL (and the follow-ups: ties, a single salary, `DENSE_RANK()` vs subquery) — and why does the interviewer care about your reasoning more than the answer?
shortTitle: Common SDET coding tasks with complexity and edge cases

s1_definition.profdef: These are standard screening problems for an SDET: find the first non-repeating character in a string, reverse a string without using built-in reversal, remove duplicates from an array and then deduplicate objects by a chosen property, and find the second-highest salary in SQL including handling ties, a single distinct value, and the choice between a window function and a subquery. Solving them well means stating the approach, the time and space complexity, and the edge cases, because the interviewer is evaluating your reasoning, how you decompose a problem, pick a data structure, analyze complexity, and handle edge cases, more than the final code.
s1_definition.analogy: These are like quick aptitude checks the National Bank of India gives an automation engineer to see how they think, not whether they memorized an answer. Can they find the first customer in a queue who appears only once, reverse an account reference by hand, collapse a list of duplicate transactions, remove duplicate customers by their account number, and work out who earns the second-highest salary even when several people tie. The interviewer watches how you reason: do you pick the right tool, do you say how fast it runs, do you remember the empty list and the all-duplicates cases. A candidate who explains their thinking clearly is more valuable than one who blurts a memorized solution, because the job is thinking through test and data problems all day.
s1_definition.oneliner: Solve first-non-repeating-char with a count map, reverse a string with a two-pointer or index loop, dedupe arrays with a set and objects with a seen-by-key set, and second-highest salary with DENSE_RANK or a subquery, always stating complexity and edge cases, because the interviewer values your reasoning over the answer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are standard screening problems for an SDET: find the first non-repeating character in a string, reverse a string without using built-in reversal, remove duplicates from an array and then deduplicate objects by a chosen property, and find the second-highest salary in SQL including handling ties, a single distinct value, and the choice between a window function and a subquery. Solving them well means stating the approach, the time and space complexity, and the edge cases, because the interviewer is evaluating your reasoning, how you decompose a problem, pick a data structure, analyze complexity, and handle edge cases, more than the final code.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** These are like quick aptitude checks the National Bank of India gives an automation engineer to see how they think, not whether they memorized an answer. Can they find the first customer in a queue who appears only once, reverse an account reference by hand, collapse a list of duplicate transactions, remove duplicate customers by their account number, and work out who earns the second-highest salary even when several people tie. The interviewer watches how you reason: do you pick the right tool, do you say how fast it runs, do you remember the empty list and the all-duplicates cases. A candidate who explains their thinking clearly is more valuable than one who blurts a memorized solution, because the job is thinking through test and data problems all day.

**One line to remember:** Solve first-non-repeating-char with a count map, reverse a string with a two-pointer or index loop, dedupe arrays with a set and objects with a seen-by-key set, and second-highest salary with DENSE_RANK or a subquery, always stating complexity and edge cases, because the interviewer values your reasoning over the answer.

sections.s2_technical:
First non-repeating character: the efficient approach makes two passes. The first pass counts each character's frequency in a map that preserves insertion order, and the second pass returns the first character whose count is one. This is linear time in the length of the string and linear space in the number of distinct characters, which is far better than a naive nested loop that is quadratic. Edge cases are an empty string, which has no answer, a string where every character repeats, which also has no answer, and case sensitivity and whitespace, which you clarify with the interviewer. Using an insertion-ordered map matters because the answer is the first such character, so order must be preserved.

Reverse a string without built-ins: you convert the string to a character array and swap from both ends toward the middle with two pointers, or build the result by iterating from the last index to the first. Either is linear time and linear space because strings are immutable and you produce a new sequence. The point of forbidding the built-in is to show you can manipulate indices and understand the mechanics. Edge cases are empty and single-character strings, which return themselves, and, if asked, awareness that naive character reversal can corrupt multi-byte or combined Unicode characters, which is a thoughtful nuance.

Remove duplicates from an array: the standard approach adds elements to a set, which gives linear time and linear space and loses original order unless you use an insertion-ordered set; if order must be preserved you iterate and add to a result only when the element was not already seen. The follow-up, dedupe objects by a specific property, cannot use plain equality because two distinct objects with the same property are different references, so you keep a set of the seen property values and include an object only the first time its key appears, again linear time and space. Edge cases are an empty array, an array with all duplicates collapsing to one, null elements or null keys, and deciding which duplicate to keep, usually the first.

Second-highest salary in SQL: the clean modern approach uses a window function, DENSE_RANK over salaries ordered descending, then selects the rows where the dense rank equals two, which naturally handles ties because tied salaries share a rank and returns nothing when there is no distinct second value. The classic subquery approach selects the maximum salary that is less than the overall maximum, which also returns the second distinct salary and yields null when there is only one distinct value. The follow-ups probe understanding: with ties you must decide whether second-highest means the second distinct salary, which DENSE_RANK gives, or the second row, which ROW_NUMBER gives; with a single salary both correct approaches return null or no row rather than erroring; and DENSE_RANK versus the subquery is a readability and generality trade-off, the window function scales cleanly to the Nth highest by changing the rank, while the subquery is simple for exactly the second.

The reason the interviewer cares about reasoning more than the answer is that these problems are proxies for the daily work of an SDET. The job is constant problem decomposition, choosing the right data structure, reasoning about complexity when a test must process large data, and anticipating edge cases, which is exactly what good testing is. A candidate who states the approach, justifies the data structure, gives the complexity, and enumerates edge cases demonstrates the thinking that transfers to designing tests, debugging failures, and writing framework utilities. A memorized answer with no explanation shows none of that and does not predict on-the-job competence. The senior nuances are to always say the complexity out loud, to clarify ambiguous requirements before coding, case sensitivity, order preservation, the meaning of second-highest, to name the edge cases proactively, and to mention the trade-offs between approaches, because articulating the reasoning is the actual thing being assessed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India needs the first transaction code character that is unique, and a reversed account reference, quickly and correctly, which maps to first-non-repeating-character and string reversal with their complexity and edge cases.

Problem 2 — A feed contains duplicate transaction identifiers and duplicate customer objects by account number that must be collapsed, which maps to array deduplication and object deduplication by property.

Problem 3 — HR needs the second-highest salary among employees, handling ties and a single salary, which maps to the DENSE_RANK and subquery SQL solutions.

In the mini-project we implement all four coding tasks in Java with explicit complexity and edge-case comments, plus the SQL for the second-highest salary, so the reasoning is visible. We present a Java harness and a SQL script.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: sample strings, arrays, customer objects, and an employees table.

Step 1: For the first non-repeating character, the code counts each character of the transaction code into an insertion-ordered map in one pass, then returns the first character with a count of one, X for the sample, and correctly returns nothing for an empty string and for an all-repeating string, with the complexity stated as linear.

Step 2: For reversing, the code swaps characters from both ends toward the middle with two pointers, turning the account reference into its reverse, and returns an empty string unchanged, again linear time.

Step 3: For array deduplication, the code adds each identifier to a set and keeps it in the result only on first sight, so the output preserves order and drops repeats, in linear time.

Step 4: For object deduplication by account number, the code keeps a set of seen account numbers and includes a customer only the first time its account number appears, so the two distinct customer objects sharing one account collapse to the first, demonstrating that equality must be on the chosen key, not the object reference.

Step 5: For the second-highest salary, the SQL shows the DENSE_RANK approach, which handles ties by treating tied salaries as the same rank and returns the second distinct salary, and the subquery approach, which returns the maximum below the overall maximum, with both returning nothing or null when there is only one distinct salary, and a note that the second-row interpretation would use ROW_NUMBER instead.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  first non-repeating: string → count map (ordered) → first count==1
       O(n) time, O(k) space; edge: empty/all-repeat → null

  reverse: string → char[] → two-pointer swap → new string
       O(n)/O(n); edge: empty/single → itself

  dedupe array: items → seen Set (add==false skips) → ordered result
       O(n)/O(n); edge: empty/all-dupes/null

  dedupe objects: items → seen KEY Set (by property) → keep first
       O(n)/O(n); edge: null key; equality on KEY not reference

  2nd-highest salary: rows → DENSE_RANK desc → rnk==2 (distinct, ties ok)
       OR MAX(salary) < MAX(salary); single salary → NULL
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I solve these four tasks the same disciplined way, stating the approach, the complexity, and the edge cases. For the first non-repeating character I make two passes: the first counts each character into an insertion-ordered map, the second returns the first character with a count of one, which is linear time and linear in the distinct characters, and the edge cases are an empty string and an all-repeating string, both of which have no answer, plus clarifying case sensitivity. For reversing a string without built-ins I convert to a character array and swap from both ends inward with two pointers, linear time and space, with empty and single-character strings returning themselves, and I mention that naive character swapping can corrupt combined Unicode as a thoughtful nuance. For removing duplicates from an array I add each element to a set and keep it only on first sight so order is preserved, linear time and space, and the follow-up to dedupe objects by a property cannot use object equality because two distinct objects can share a property, so I keep a set of seen key values and include an object only the first time its key appears. For the second-highest salary I use DENSE_RANK ordered descending and select rank two, which handles ties by treating tied salaries as one rank and returns the second distinct salary, or the classic subquery selecting the maximum salary below the overall maximum, and I note that a single distinct salary yields null, and that if second-highest must mean the second row rather than the second distinct value I would use ROW_NUMBER instead.

The reason the interviewer cares about my reasoning more than the answer is that these problems are proxies for the daily work of an SDET: constant problem decomposition, choosing the right data structure, reasoning about complexity when a test must process large data, and anticipating edge cases, which is exactly what good testing is. A candidate who clarifies the ambiguous requirement, justifies the data structure, states the complexity out loud, and names the edge cases proactively demonstrates the thinking that transfers to designing tests, debugging failures, and writing framework utilities, whereas a memorized answer with no explanation predicts nothing about on-the-job competence.

At the National Bank of India these exact patterns showed up in real work, dedupe-by-property when collapsing duplicate customer records by account number, and a DENSE_RANK query for ranking, and in each case the valuable part was reasoning about ties, nulls, and order, not recalling syntax. So in an interview I deliberately narrate my thinking, clarify, choose, analyze, and enumerate edges, because showing how I reason is the thing actually being assessed.
